# XML Parsing Attack

This example demonstrates an XML entity-expansion denial-of-service attack,
often called the "billion laughs" pattern.

The code is intentionally small. That is deliberate. The lesson is not hidden
in application complexity, but in the fact that a tiny XML document can expand
into a much larger in-memory structure when the parser accepts nested entity
definitions from untrusted input.

In other words: structured input is still untrusted input. If you let a parser
do expensive work on behalf of an attacker, the parser itself becomes part of
your attack surface.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- how recursive XML entities amplify a small payload into a much larger DOM
- why XML parsing can become a denial-of-service problem even when the Java
  code looks harmless
- what the JDK's entity-expansion limit is protecting you from
- why raising parser limits for attacker-controlled XML is a risky workaround
- what safer production guidance looks like when handling XML from untrusted
  sources

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

## Build the example

Compile the project before running the parser examples.

We use `compile` rather than `package` because the lesson is about parser
behaviour, not about creating a distributable artifact. Compiling once gives
you the classes under `target/classes`, which is all the walkthrough needs.

What you gain from this step: a clean, repeatable baseline before you start
comparing parser behaviour.

```shell
./mvnw clean compile
```

Build output

```
...
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
...
```

## Inspect the payload structure

Start by reading the XML payload used by `AllTheLolz`.

Each entity is defined in terms of the previous one, repeated ten times. That
means the growth is multiplicative rather than linear.

What you gain from this step: you see why the document is dangerous before you
run any Java code.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ELEMENT lolz (#PCDATA)>
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
 <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
 <!ENTITY lol4 "&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;">
 <!ENTITY lol5 "&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;">
 <!ENTITY lol6 "&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;">
 <!ENTITY lol7 "&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;">
 <!ENTITY lol8 "&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;">
 <!ENTITY lol9 "&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;">
]>
<lolz>&lol4;</lolz>

<!-- called the "billion LOLs attack: <lolz>&lol9</lolz> would generate 6 x 10^9, or 1 billion LOLs -->
```

The files `lol2.xml`, `lol3.xml`, and `lol4.xml` follow the same pattern but
stop at smaller expansion levels. They exist so you can observe the growth
gradually instead of jumping straight to the largest payload in the example.

## Inspect the parser code

Now inspect the Java code.

`AllTheLolz` parses `lol.xml` using a plain `DocumentBuilderFactory` and then
walks the DOM tree to count how much text was produced.

What you gain from this step: you see that the vulnerability is not in complex
application logic. It comes from trusting the parser to expand
attacker-controlled entities.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilder;
import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory;
import javax.xml.parsers.ParserConfigurationException;

import org.w3c.dom.Document;
import org.w3c.dom.Node;
import org.xml.sax.SAXException;

/**
 * Hello world!
 *
 */
public final class AllTheLolz {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws SAXException, IOException, ParserConfigurationException {
        DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
        DocumentBuilder db = dbf.newDocumentBuilder();

        Document doc = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol.xml"));
        System.out.println("lol generated " + inventory(doc) + " characters.");
    }

    // depth-first traversal of the resulting document tree, using recursion.
    private static int inventory(Node document) {
        int n = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < document.getChildNodes().getLength(); ++i) {
            Node node = document.getChildNodes().item(i);
            if (node.getTextContent() != null) {
                n += node.getTextContent().length();
            }
            n += inventory(node);
        }
        return n;
    }
}
```

`Lolz` performs the same parsing work against `lol2.xml`, `lol3.xml`, and
`lol4.xml` so you can observe how quickly the expansion grows.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilder;
import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory;
import javax.xml.parsers.ParserConfigurationException;

import org.w3c.dom.Document;
import org.w3c.dom.Node;
import org.xml.sax.SAXException;

/**
 * Hello world!
 *
 */
public final class Lolz {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws SAXException, IOException, ParserConfigurationException {
        DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
        DocumentBuilder db = dbf.newDocumentBuilder();

        Document doc2 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol2.xml"));
        Document doc3 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol3.xml"));
        Document doc4 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol4.xml"));

        System.out.println("lol_2 generated " + inventory(doc2) + " characters.");
        System.out.println("lol_3 generated " + inventory(doc3) + " characters.");
        System.out.println("lol_4 generated " + inventory(doc4) + " characters.");
    }

    // depth-first traversal of the resulting document tree, using recursion.
    private static int inventory(Node document) {
        int n = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < document.getChildNodes().getLength(); ++i) {
            Node node = document.getChildNodes().item(i);
            if (node.getTextContent() != null) {
                n += node.getTextContent().length();
            }
            n += inventory(node);
        }
        return n;
    }
}
```

## Run the bounded expansions deliberately

Run `Lolz` with a higher entity-expansion limit so the parser is allowed to
materialise the smaller payloads.

We raise the limit here only for demonstration purposes. On recent JDKs, the
default limit is intentionally low enough that these payloads may already be
blocked. That is a feature, not an inconvenience.

What you gain from this step: a controlled view of the amplification effect
before you look at the protective guardrail.

```shell
java -Djdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit=300000 --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse.Lolz
```

Observed output

```
lol_2 generated 600 characters.
lol_3 generated 6000 characters.
lol_4 generated 60000 characters.
```

Each step multiplies the expanded text dramatically. The Java code is simple,
but the parser is doing increasingly expensive work on behalf of the input.

That is the secure-coding lesson: expensive parsing work can be
attacker-controlled even when your own code does nothing more than
"parse and print".

## Observe the parser guardrail

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse.AllTheLolz
```

Expected parser failure

```
[Fatal Error] :1:1: JAXP00010001: The parser has encountered more than "2500" entity expansions in this document; this is the limit imposed by "jdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit".
Exception in thread "main" org.xml.sax.SAXParseException; lineNumber: 1; columnNumber: 1; JAXP00010001: The parser has encountered more than "2500" entity expansions in this document; this is the limit imposed by "jdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit".
    at java.xml/com.sun.org.apache.xerces.internal.parsers.DOMParser.parse(DOMParser.java:263)
    at java.xml/com.sun.org.apache.xerces.internal.jaxp.DocumentBuilderImpl.parse(DocumentBuilderImpl.java:335)
    at java.xml/javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilder.parse(DocumentBuilder.java:206)
    at com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse.AllTheLolz.main(AllTheLolz.java:23)
```

On recent JDKs, this run should fail with an entity-expansion-limit error. The
exact numeric limit can vary by runtime. What matters is the meaning of the
error: the parser stopped expanding entities before the document could grow
further.

What you gain from this step: you see that modern JDKs include a built-in safety
barrier against this class of attack.

Also notice the property name reported by the runtime. Older examples often use
`entityExpansionLimit`, while newer JDKs report the more explicit
`jdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit`. For Java 21 or newer, prefer the fully qualified
property name in your documentation and troubleshooting notes.

## Override the limit to understand the risk

Now run the same parser again, but explicitly raise the limit.

We do this to prove a security point, not because it is a good production
practice. If you increase parser limits for attacker-controlled XML, you may
simply be re-enabling the denial-of-service path that the JDK was trying to
block.

What you gain from this step: you see how a configuration change can undo a
useful safety control.

```shell
java -Djdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit=300000 --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.xml_parse.AllTheLolz
```

Observed output

```
lol generated 60096 characters.
```

With the higher limit in place, the parser accepts the same payload.

That successful run is not the safe outcome. It is evidence that the parser was
allowed to perform a large amount of expansion work from a tiny input document.

Safer production guidance is:

- reject DTDs and entity declarations entirely when your application does not
  need them
- keep parser security settings explicit instead of relying on accidental
  defaults
- do not raise expansion limits just to make untrusted XML "work"

## What this example teaches

- XML is not automatically safe just because it is structured.
- Nested entity expansion can turn a very small payload into expensive parser
  work.
- The JDK's entity-expansion limit is a security control, not a nuisance to
  disable.
- Relaxing parser limits for untrusted XML can reintroduce denial-of-service
  risk.
- Secure coding includes understanding parser behaviour, not only validating
  business fields.
